Reliability Statistics

Source: R/reli_stats.R
reli_stats.Rd

reli_stats() and reli_aov() return the intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), the coefficient of variation (CV), and the standard errors of measurement (SEM), estimate (SEE) and prediction (SEP) described by Weir (2005), all at once.

These functions are superseded: they still work, but new code should use icc_test() for an ICC (with a test against a meaningful null value and optional bootstrap inference) and reli_err_test() for the SEM, SEE or SEP, including the CV via scale = "log" (sympercents) or scale = "mean". See Details for how the two sets of functions differ.

Usage

reli_stats(
  measure = NULL,
  item = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  data,
  wide = FALSE,
  col.names = NULL,
  se_type = c("MSE", "ICC1", "ICC2", "ICC3", "ICC1k", "ICC2k", "ICC3k"),
  cv_calc = c("MSE", "residuals", "SEM"),
  conf.level = 0.95,
  other_ci = FALSE,
  type = c("chisq", "perc", "norm", "basic"),
  replicates = 1999
)

reli_aov(
  measure = NULL,
  item = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  data,
  wide = FALSE,
  col.names = NULL,
  se_type = c("MSE", "ICC1", "ICC2", "ICC3", "ICC1k", "ICC2k", "ICC3k"),
  cv_calc = c("MSE", "residuals", "SEM"),
  conf.level = 0.95,
  other_ci = FALSE,
  type = c("chisq", "perc", "norm", "basic"),
  replicates = 1999
)

Arguments

measure

Name of column containing the measurement of interest.

item

Name of column containing the items. If this is a test-retest reliability study then this would indicate the time point (e.g., time1, time2, time3, etc.).

id

Column with subject identifier.

data

Data frame with all data.

wide

Logical value (TRUE or FALSE) indicating if data is in a "wide" format. Default is FALSE.

col.names

If wide is equal to TRUE then col.names is a list of the column names containing the measurements for reliability analysis.

se_type

Type of standard error calculation. The default, "MSE", uses the error mean square for the SEM, and ICC3 (ICC(C,1)) for the SEE and SEP. Otherwise, the SD of all the measurements and the named ICC are used for all three (see Details).

cv_calc

Coefficient of variation (CV) calculation: "MSE" (default), the square root of the error mean square divided by the grand mean, or "SEM", the SEM (see se_type) divided by the grand mean. "residuals" is no longer supported and is replaced by "MSE" with a warning.

conf.level

The confidence level required. Default is 95%. The ICC intervals are two-sided (see Details).

other_ci

Logical value (TRUE or FALSE) indicating whether to calculate confidence intervals for the CV, SEM, SEP, and SEE.

type

The type of confidence intervals for the CV, SEM, SEP, and SEE: "chisq" (default; analytic intervals, see Details), or a bootstrap interval, "perc" (percentile), "norm" (normal, with bias correction) or "basic".

replicates

The number of bootstrap replicates. Default is 1999.

Value

Returns single list with the results of the reliability analysis.

  • icc: Table of ICC results

  • lmer: The fitted model: a linear mixed model from lme4 (reli_stats()), or a linear model of subjects and items (reli_aov())

  • anova: Analysis of Variance table (mean squares reconstructed from the variance components for reli_stats())

  • var_comp: Table of Variance Components

  • n.id: Number of subjects/participants

  • n.item: Number of items/time points

  • cv: Coefficient of Variation (a one-row data frame)

  • SEM: Standard Error of Measurement (a one-row data frame)

  • SEE: Standard Error of the Estimate (a one-row data frame)

  • SEP: Standard Error of Prediction (a one-row data frame)

  • call: the matched call, with the settings used

Details

Estimation. Both functions use the engine of icc_test(): reli_stats() fits a linear mixed model by REML (crossed random effects for subjects and items) and allows missing measurements; reli_aov() uses the analysis of variance and keeps only subjects measured on every item (incomplete subjects are dropped with a message). With complete data the two give the same results (unless a variance component is estimated at zero). With missing data, reli_stats() uses degrees of freedom based on the observed data and warns that its intervals are approximate.

ICCs. The six forms of Shrout and Fleiss (1979) are returned, with the F-based intervals of McGraw and Wong (1996). The intervals are two-sided conf.level intervals, as in those papers (and in the psych, irr, SPSS and Stata implementations). Before version 0.4.0 the intervals used conf.level in each tail, so each limit was a one-sided conf.level bound and the pair covered only 1 - 2 * (1 - conf.level); the old output at conf.level = c is reproduced by conf.level = 1 - 2 * (1 - c) (e.g. old 0.95 = new 0.90). For a one-sided lower bound on a single ICC, use icc_test(alternative = "greater").

SEM, SEE and SEP. With se_type = "MSE", SEM = \(\sqrt{MS_E}\) (Weir, 2005, preferred), and SEE = \(SD\sqrt{ICC(1 - ICC)}\) and SEP = \(SD\sqrt{1 - ICC^2}\) with ICC3. With another se_type, the named ICC is used for all three, and SEM = \(SD\sqrt{1 - ICC}\). Here SD is the SD of all the measurements, \(\sqrt{SS_{total}/(N - 1)}\), as in Weir (2005). reli_err_test() instead uses the SD matched to the ICC's denominator, so its SEE and SEP differ slightly. A negative ICC is treated as zero.

CV. The CV is the SEM (or \(\sqrt{MS_E}\)) divided by the grand mean, as a proportion (printed as a percentage).

Intervals for the CV, SEM, SEE and SEP (other_ci = TRUE). With type = "chisq", the SEM from \(MS_E\) has the exact \(\chi^2\) interval; every other statistic has a Wald interval on the log scale with a delta-method standard error from the normal-theory variances of the mean squares (and of the grand mean, for the CV). Before version 0.4.0 these used \(\chi^2\) intervals with the error degrees of freedom (and Vangel's interval for the CV), which do not apply to these statistics. The bootstrap types resample subjects (as icc_test() does, including its hybrid step for the item mean square); before version 0.4.0 reli_stats() used a parametric bootstrap.

References

Weir, J. P. (2005). Quantifying test-retest reliability using the intraclass correlation coefficient and the SEM. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 19(1), 231-240. doi:10.1519/15184.1

Shrout, P. E., & Fleiss, J. L. (1979). Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability. Psychological Bulletin, 86(2), 420-428. doi:10.1037/0033-2909.86.2.420

McGraw, K. O., & Wong, S. P. (1996). Forming inferences about some intraclass correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 1(1), 30-46. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.1.1.30

See also

icc_test(), reli_err_test()

Examples

data('reps')
reli_stats(data = reps, wide = TRUE, col.names = c("x","y"))
#> Only 2 items in data. It is recommended to use reli_aov instead of reli_stats.
#> Warning: 5.0% of subject-by-item cells are missing. Intervals use observed-data degrees of freedom and are approximate; consider icc_test(method = "reml", boot = TRUE).
#> 
#> Coefficient of Variation (%):  15.8
#> Standard Error of Measurement (SEM):  0.863
#> Standard Error of the Estimate (SEE):  0.639
#> Standard Error of Prediction (SEP):  1.08
#> 
#> Intraclass Correlation Coefficients with  95 % C.I.
#>            Model         Measures  Type    ICC Lower CI Upper CI
#> 1 one-way random        Agreement  ICC1 0.4956  0.05599   0.7682
#> 2 two-way random        Agreement  ICC2 0.5097  0.09605   0.7726
#> 3  two-way fixed      Consistency  ICC3 0.5384  0.10441   0.7925
#> 4 one-way random   Avg. Agreement ICC1k 0.6627  0.10603   0.8689
#> 5 two-way random   Avg. Agreement ICC2k 0.6753  0.17526   0.8717
#> 6  two-way fixed Avg. Consistency ICC3k 0.7000  0.18908   0.8842
#> 

# The recommended replacements (reps has missing measurements, so REML)
icc_test(data = reps, col.names = c("x", "y"), method = "reml")
#> Warning: 5.0% of subject-by-item cells are missing. Intervals and p-values use observed-data degrees of freedom and are approximate; they may be liberal as missingness increases. Consider boot = TRUE.
#> 
#> 	Two-way, consistency, single-measure ICC [Shrout & Fleiss ICC(3,1)]
#> 	(REML)
#> 
#> data:  x, y
#> 
#> alternative hypothesis: two.sided
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.1044136 0.7924971
#> sample estimates:
#>  ICC(C,1) 
#> 0.5384325 
#> 
reli_err_test(data = reps, col.names = c("x", "y"), method = "reml")
#> Warning: 5.0% of subject-by-item cells are missing. Intervals and p-values use observed-data degrees of freedom and are approximate; they may be liberal as missingness increases. Consider boot = TRUE.
#> 
#> 	Standard error of measurement (two-way, consistency) (REML)
#> 
#> data:  x, y
#> 
#> alternative hypothesis: two.sided
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.6478589 1.2943096
#> sample estimates:
#>       SEM 
#> 0.8633657 
#>
